news.title: 172-year-old bank sees 400% upside for 'federal bank' token
news.summary: 172-year-old bank sees 400% upside for 'federal bank' token
news.full_text:
Sky Protocol, earlier known as MakerDAO, is a decentralized finance (DeFi) project built on Ethereum.

The crypto project is best known for its USDS stablecoin. Pegged 1:1 to the U.S. dollar, USDS attempts to keep its value the same as that of the dollar.

As per the onchain analytics platform DeFiLlama, USDS has a market cap of more than $6 billion and accounts for over 2% of the total stablecoin market.

Sky Protocol's governance token, SKY, gives holders the right to vote on the protocol's future. With a market cap of $1.38 billion, SKY is the 62nd largest cryptocurrency.

On Sep. 11, Standard Chartered initiated coverage of the SKY token with a price target of $0.325 by the end of 2028.

The 172-year-old bank's global head of digital assets research, Geoff Kendrick, compared the Sky Protocol to a "federal bank" as the crypto project issues stablecoins, has a governance framework, and lends assets at a wholesale interest rate. In fact, Sky is also the largest issuer of yield-bearing stablecoins.

Sky lets users stake the USDS stablecoin in exchange for the sUSDS token. Not only does the user earn the staking rewards on their USDS holding, they can also deploy the sUSDS token across the DeFi ecosystem.

As per DeFiLlama, sUSDS has a total value locked of $4.59 billion and offers an annual percentage yield (APY) of 3.6%.

news.title: AI Agents Create Their Own Monitoring Problem. Datadog and Dynatrace Are Racing to Own It
news.summary: AI Agents Create Their Own Monitoring Problem. Datadog and Dynatrace Are Racing to Own It
news.full_text:
AI coding agents are supposed to make software cheaper to build. They may also create more software changes, production failures and machine-generated complexity to inspect. That second-order effect connects Datadog, Inc. (NASDAQ:DDOG) and Dynatrace, Inc. (NYSE:DT) to an observability market that AI could expand rather than erase.

Datadog told the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 10 that monetization of AI-agent observability has begun, with thousands of customers using the capability. Management described an emerging "inference economy": more AI applications and agents mean more activity that customers need to monitor. That shifts the opportunity from watching human-written releases toward tracing continuous decisions made by software that can change software itself.

One day later, Dynatrace launched a verified Cursor Marketplace plugin. A single installation gives coding agents access to live production context through MCP and 30 Dynatrace skills. The timing makes the competition tangible: Datadog is framing the category, while Dynatrace is putting production telemetry directly inside an agent's workflow.

Datadog has the stronger recent growth profile. Second-quarter revenue rose 36% to $1.12 billion, and customers generating at least $100,000 of annual recurring revenue increased 23% to roughly 4,720. Its usage-based model can capture expanding telemetry and inference volume. The risk is the same sensitivity to optimization that has periodically hurt cloud vendors; more capable agents could also resolve some incidents.

Dynatrace offers a different defense. It prices the Cursor integration on data consumption rather than per user, reducing direct exposure to shrinking developer-seat counts. Its latest quarterly ARR grew 17% to $2.136 billion, while annualized log-consumption reached $200 million after almost doubling over the previous two quarters. Slower companywide growth, plus the planned $915 million Arize acquisition, raises execution and integration risk.

Insider Monkey's hedge fund database counted 92 hedge funds holding DDOG in Q2 2026, up from 80 in Q1; Arrowstreet Capital held 2,195,554 shares after increasing its stake 40%. DT holders rose to 48 from 46, while AQR Capital Management owned 8,317,467 shares after a 346% increase. Those quarter-end snapshots predate the September announcements.

As of August 31, 10,220,303 DDOG shares were sold short, equal to 3.04% of float and 2.94 days of average volume. That modest bearish position alone does not settle the thesis. The deciding question is whether autonomous agents prevent enough problems to reduce monitoring, or create enough software activity to make observability a larger machine-to-machine market.

While we acknowledge the potential of DDOG and DT as investments, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. news.title: GE Aerospace (GE)’s $12 Billion CPP Acquisition Puts Its Growth Strategy to the Test
news.summary: GE Aerospace (GE)’s $12 Billion CPP Acquisition Puts Its Growth Strategy to the Test
news.full_text:
GE Aerospace (NYSE:GE) is making its largest acquisition since becoming a standalone publicly traded company. It agreed to acquire Consolidated Precision Products (CPP) for around $12 billion.

CPP is one of the world's largest precision castings providers. It's a major GE supplier. Precision castings is a major pressure point for the aerospace engines industry. Acquiring CPP would give GE Aerospace greater control over a critical part of its engine supply chain.

And the deal could strengthen GE's ability to meet demand already sitting in its backlog. But the investment case depends on whether additional production capacity generates enough free cash flow to justify the deal's premium price.

Engine manufacturers like GE Aerospace (NYSE:GE) are struggling to keep pace with surging demand due to supply chain constraints. CPP is a major supplier of precision castings for GE's LEAP and GEnx engines. GE plans to raise CPP's output. It would do that by improving factory yields and machine use. With the CPP deal, GE also ​sees a path to accelerate production of new engine technologies.

The timing is important as GE already has substantial demand to fulfill. The company reported a backlog of more than $210 billion in the latest quarter. That backlog includes over $170 billion in commercial services. About 70% of CPP's revenue comes from commercial and defense engines. That makes the acquisition closely aligned with GE Aerospace's core markets. GE expects CPP to generate around $2 billion in revenue in 2027.

The strategic rationale of the CPP acquisition does not automatically make the deal financially attractive. Consider that GE values CPP at about 26 times expected 2027 EBITDA before net synergies.

GE Aerospace (NYSE:GE) will fund the acquisition with a mix of cash on hand and debt. The company expects the acquisition to be accretive to adjusted earnings and free cash flow in the first year, excluding certain items.

GE needs higher factory yields and greater production efficiency to translate the acquisition into stronger financial results. If CPP helps GE produce more engines from the existing demand pipeline, the benefits could extend beyond initial engine sales to an expanded installed base that in turn supports recurring aftermarket business.
